claim: Humans are sexually dimorphic: men and women differ in body build and composition, craniofacial structure, and voice pitch, likely mediated in part by developmental testosterone.
source: Humans are sexually dimorphic: men and women differ in body build and composition, craniofacial structure, and voice pitch, likely mediated in part by developmental testosterone.
evidence: This is a general statement about human sexual dimorphism that draws on established scientific knowledge about sex differences.

claim: Voice pitch, height, and testosterone all predicted mating outcomes in the meta-analysis.
source: Voice pitch, height, and testosterone all predicted mating; however, strength/muscularity was the strongest and only consistent predictor of both mating and reproduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the meta-analytic data presented in the study.

claim: Strength/muscularity was the strongest and only consistent predictor of both mating and reproduction.
source: Voice pitch, height, and testosterone all predicted mating; however, strength/muscularity was the strongest and only consistent predictor of both mating and reproduction.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the meta-analytic results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Facial masculinity did not significantly predict mating or reproductive outcomes.
source: Facial masculinity and digit ratios did not significantly predict either.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Digit ratios (2D:4D) did not significantly predict mating or reproductive outcomes.
source: Facial masculinity and digit ratios did not significantly predict either.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: There was no clear evidence for any effects of masculinity on offspring viability.
source: There was no clear evidence for any effects of masculinity on offspring viability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the meta-analytic results.

claim: Humans are a sexually dimorphic species.
source: Humans are a sexually dimorphic species (Plavcan, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Sexual selection in mammalian species is commonly argued to have acted more strongly on male traits due to greater variance in males' reproductive output.
source: Sexual selection in mammalian species, including human and non-human primates, is commonly argued to have acted more strongly on male traits, as a consequence of greater variance in males' reproductive output (Hammer et al., 2008) and a male-biased operational sex ratio, that is a surplus of reproductively available males relative to fertile females (e.g. Mitani et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Men are, on average, 7–8% taller than women.
source: Men are, on average, 7–8% taller than women (Gray and Wolfe, 1980) and weigh approximately 15% more (Smith and Jungers, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Men weigh approximately 15% more than women.
source: Men are, on average, 7–8% taller than women (Gray and Wolfe, 1980) and weigh approximately 15% more (Smith and Jungers, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Compared to women, men have 61% more overall muscle mass and 90% greater upper body strength.
source: Relative to this fairly modest body size dimorphism, upper body musculature and strength are highly dimorphic in humans: compared to women, men have 61% more overall muscle mass, and 90% greater upper body strength (Lassek and Gaulin, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Men's 2D:4D is typically lower than women's.
source: Second-to-fourth finger (digit) length ratios are often claimed to be sexually dimorphic, with men's 2D:4D typically being lower than women's (Manning, 2002, although this may not be universal: Apicella et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research, with a caveat that it may not be universal.

claim: Fundamental frequency (voice pitch) is nearly six standard deviations lower in men than in women.
source: In addition, fundamental frequency, commonly referred to as voice pitch, is nearly six standard deviations lower in men than in women (Puts et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The development of masculine traits in men is influenced by exposure to androgens, particularly testosterone.
source: The development of these masculine traits in men is influenced by exposure to androgens, particularly testosterone.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the biological basis of masculine trait development.

claim: 2D:4D is commonly claimed to be influenced primarily by prenatal testosterone levels and is present at birth.
source: With the exception of 2D:4D, which is commonly claimed to be influenced primarily by prenatal testosterone levels and is present at birth (Galis et al., 2010; but see Richards et al., 2019), masculine traits generally develop or become exaggerated following a surge in testosterone production at sexual maturity (Butterfield et al., 2009; Fechner, 2003; Weston et al., 2007) – although it is not necessarily clear whether the size of that surge corresponds directly to the extent of trait expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research, with a caveat citation suggesting controversy.

claim: Masculine traits generally develop or become exaggerated following a surge in testosterone production at sexual maturity.
source: With the exception of 2D:4D, which is commonly claimed to be influenced primarily by prenatal testosterone levels and is present at birth (Galis et al., 2010; but see Richards et al., 2019), masculine traits generally develop or become exaggerated following a surge in testosterone production at sexual maturity (Butterfield et al., 2009; Fechner, 2003; Weston et al., 2007) – although it is not necessarily clear whether the size of that surge corresponds directly to the extent of trait expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: According to the immunocompetence handicap hypothesis, masculine traits are a costly signal of heritable immunocompetence due to the putative immunosuppressive properties of testosterone.
source: Firstly, according to the immunocompetence handicap hypothesis (Folstad and Karter, 1992), masculine traits are a costly signal of heritable immunocompetence, that is good genetic quality, due to the putative immunosuppressive properties of testosterone (see Muehlenbein and Bribiescas, 2005).
evidence: This claim describes a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The immunocompetence handicap hypothesis predicts that masculine men should produce healthier and more viable offspring.
source: Masculine men should therefore produce healthier and more viable offspring, who are more likely to survive.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the immunocompetence handicap hypothesis described in the text.

claim: The relationship between testosterone and health is complex.
source: While beyond the scope of this article, common criticisms include that the relationship between testosterone and health is complex (Nowak et al., 2018), and facial masculinity is inconsistently linked to health (e.g. Boothroyd et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2020; Marcinkowska et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2013; Zaidi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Facial masculinity is inconsistently linked to health.
source: While beyond the scope of this article, common criticisms include that the relationship between testosterone and health is complex (Nowak et al., 2018), and facial masculinity is inconsistently linked to health (e.g. Boothroyd et al., 2013; Foo et al., 2020; Marcinkowska et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2013; Zaidi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Evidence is mixed regarding whether women are attracted to masculinity in men's faces.
source: Evidence is similarly mixed regarding the key assumption that women are attracted to masculinity in men's faces (Boothroyd et al., 2013; Zeigler-Hill et al., 2015) and bodies (Frederick and Haselton, 2007; Gray and Frederick, 2012; Lukaszewski et al., 2014; Sell et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Under the male-male competition hypothesis, formidable men are better equipped to compete with other men for resources, status, and partners.
source: Secondly, under the male-male competition hypothesis, authors have argued that formidable (i.e. physically strong and imposing) men are better equipped to compete with other men for resources, status, and partners (Hill et al., 2016; Puts, 2016), through e.g. direct physical contests or by deterring rivals indirectly (Hill et al., 2016; Sell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Increased musculature may intimidate competitors by signaling fighting prowess and strength.
source: For instance, increased musculature may intimidate competitors by signaling fighting prowess (Sell et al., 2009) and strength (Durkee et al., 2018), while facial masculinity and voice pitch may also have an indirect relationship with perceived formidability (Butovskaya et al., 2018; Haselhuhn et al., 2015; Raine et al., 2018; Little et al., 2015; Puts and Aung, 2019; Scott et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The male-male competition hypothesis predicts that formidable men will acquire more partners over their lifetime, which will result in more offspring.
source: However, regardless of whether the driving mechanism is intra- or intersexual selection (or a combination thereof), the male-male competition hypothesis predicts that formidable men will acquire more partners over their lifetime, which will in turn result in more offspring.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the male-male competition hypothesis described in the text.

claim: Proponents of both the immunocompetence and male-male competition hypotheses have suggested that more masculine men may show reduced investment in romantic relationships and in offspring.
source: It can be noted that proponents of both the immunocompetence and male-male competition hypotheses have also suggested that more masculine men may show reduced investment in romantic relationships and in offspring (Booth and Dabbs, 1993; Boothroyd et al., 2007; Muller et al., 2008; Schild et al., 2020), potentially suppressing offspring health/survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The relationship between men's testosterone levels in adolescence and in adulthood is exceedingly weak.
source: Two important caveats here, however, are that the relationship between men's testosterone levels in adolescence (when most masculine traits become exaggerated) and in adulthood is exceedingly weak (van Bokhoven et al., 2006), and masculine trait expression in adulthood is not consistently correlated with adult testosterone levels (e.g. Lefevre et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Masculine trait expression in adulthood is not consistently correlated with adult testosterone levels.
source: Two important caveats here, however, are that the relationship between men's testosterone levels in adolescence (when most masculine traits become exaggerated) and in adulthood is exceedingly weak (van Bokhoven et al., 2006), and masculine trait expression in adulthood is not consistently correlated with adult testosterone levels (e.g. Lefevre et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Monogamous cultures do not typically show greater variance in men's versus women's reproductive success.
source: For instance, monogamous cultures do not typically show greater variance in men's versus women's reproductive success (Brown et al., 2009) and while increasing numbers of sexual partners (e.g. in serially monogamous or polygynous cultures) may often be important for increasing male reproductive success, the inverse is true amongst the Pimbwe where women are more advantaged by increased numbers of partners (Borgerhoff Mulder, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Amongst the Pimbwe, women are more advantaged by increased numbers of partners than men.
source: For instance, monogamous cultures do not typically show greater variance in men's versus women's reproductive success (Brown et al., 2009) and while increasing numbers of sexual partners (e.g. in serially monogamous or polygynous cultures) may often be important for increasing male reproductive success, the inverse is true amongst the Pimbwe where women are more advantaged by increased numbers of partners (Borgerhoff Mulder, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Van Dongen and Sprengers (2012) meta-analyzed the relationships between men's handgrip strength and sexual behavior in three industrialized populations, showing a weak, positive association (r = 0.24).
source: Van Dongen and Sprengers, 2012 meta-analyzed the relationships between men's handgrip strength (HGS) and sexual behavior in only three industrialized populations (showing a weak, positive association [r = 0.24]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior meta-analysis.

claim: Von Rueden and Jaeggi (2016) found that male status weakly predicted reproductive success across 33 non-industrialized societies (overall r = 0.19).
source: Across 33 non-industrialized societies, von Rueden and Jaeggi, 2016 found that male status (which included, but was not limited to, measures of height and strength) weakly predicted reproductive success (overall r = 0.19).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior meta-analysis.

claim: Xu et al. (2018) reported no significant association between men's height and offspring numbers across 16 studies.
source: In contrast, Xu and colleagues (Xu et al., 2018) reported no significant association between men's height and offspring numbers across 16 studies when analyzing both industrialized and non-industrialized populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior meta-analysis.

claim: Grebe et al. (2019) found that men with high levels of circulating testosterone invested more in mating effort (r = 0.22).
source: Lastly, Grebe and colleagues' (Grebe et al., 2019) meta-analysis of 16 effects – the majority of which came from Western samples – showed that men with high levels of circulating testosterone, assayed by blood or saliva, invested more in mating effort, indexed by mating with more partners and showing greater interest in casual sex (r = 0.22).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior meta-analysis.

claim: The meta-analysis included 96 studies comprising 474 effect sizes from 99 samples and 177,044 unique participants.
source: Honekopp et al., 2006), comprising 474 effect sizes from 99 samples and 177,044 unique participants (Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data included in the current meta-analysis.

claim: Global masculinity was weakly but significantly associated with greater total fitness (r = 0.080, 95% CI: [0.061, 0.101], q = 0.001).
source: In the initial overall analyses, global masculinity was weakly but significantly associated with greater total fitness (i.e. mating, reproduction, and offspring mortality combined) (r = 0.080, 95% CI: [0.061, 0.101], q = 0.001; we reiterate here that for all analyses, q-values < 0.05 denote significance after correcting for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Global masculinity significantly predicted mating outcomes (r = 0.090, 95% CI: [0.071, 0.110], q = 0.001).
source: When we divided the outcome measures into their three domains, the positive (albeit weak) associations with global masculinity remained significant for mating, but not for reproduction or offspring mortality (mating: r = 0.090, 95% CI: [0.071, 0.110], q = 0.001; reproduction: r = 0.047, 95% CI: [0.004, 0.090], q = 0.080; offspring mortality: r = .002, 95% CI: [–0.011, 0.015], q = 0.475).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Global masculinity did not significantly predict reproduction (r = 0.047, 95% CI: [0.004, 0.090], q = 0.080).
source: When we divided the outcome measures into their three domains, the positive (albeit weak) associations with global masculinity remained significant for mating, but not for reproduction or offspring mortality (mating: r = 0.090, 95% CI: [0.071, 0.110], q = 0.001; reproduction: r = 0.047, 95% CI: [0.004, 0.090], q = 0.080; offspring mortality: r = .002, 95% CI: [–0.011, 0.015], q = 0.475).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Global masculinity did not significantly predict offspring mortality (r = 0.002, 95% CI: [–0.011, 0.015], q = 0.475).
source: When we divided the outcome measures into their three domains, the positive (albeit weak) associations with global masculinity remained significant for mating, but not for reproduction or offspring mortality (mating: r = 0.090, 95% CI: [0.071, 0.110], q = 0.001; reproduction: r = 0.047, 95% CI: [0.004, 0.090], q = 0.080; offspring mortality: r = .002, 95% CI: [–0.011, 0.015], q = 0.475).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Body masculinity showed the strongest association with the mating domain (r = 0.133, 95% CI: [0.091, 0.176], q = 0.001).
source: The strongest associations with the mating domain were seen in terms of body masculinity (r = 0.133, 95% CI: [0.091, 0.176], q = 0.001; Figure 2), voice pitch (r = 0.132, 95% CI: [0.061, 0.204], q = 0.002; Figure 3), and testosterone levels (r = 0.093, 95% CI: [0.066, 0.121], q = 0.001; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Voice pitch showed a strong association with the mating domain (r = 0.132, 95% CI: [0.061, 0.204], q = 0.002).
source: The strongest associations with the mating domain were seen in terms of body masculinity (r = 0.133, 95% CI: [0.091, 0.176], q = 0.001; Figure 2), voice pitch (r = 0.132, 95% CI: [0.061, 0.204], q = 0.002; Figure 3), and testosterone levels (r = 0.093, 95% CI: [0.066, 0.121], q = 0.001; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Testosterone levels showed a strong association with the mating domain (r = 0.093, 95% CI: [0.066, 0.121], q = 0.001).
source: The strongest associations with the mating domain were seen in terms of body masculinity (r = 0.133, 95% CI: [0.091, 0.176], q = 0.001; Figure 2), voice pitch (r = 0.132, 95% CI: [0.061, 0.204], q = 0.002; Figure 3), and testosterone levels (r = 0.093, 95% CI: [0.066, 0.121], q = 0.001; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Height showed a significant but smaller effect on mating (r = 0.057, 95% CI: [0.027, 0.087], q = 0.002).
source: Height showed a significant but smaller effect size (r = 0.057, 95% CI: [0.027, 0.087], q = 0.002; Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The relationship between facial masculinity and mating was nonsignificant (r = 0.080, 95% CI: [–0.003, 0.164], q = 0.117).
source: While not the weakest association, the relationship between facial masculinity and mating was nonsignificant (r = 0.080, 95% CI: [–0.003, 0.164], q = 0.117).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: The effect of 2D:4D on mating was nonsignificant (r = 0.034, 95% CI: [0.000, 0.069], q = 0.102).
source: The effect for 2D:4D was also nonsignificant (r = 0.034, 95% CI: [0.000, 0.069], q = 0.102), and moderation analyses showed that this was the only trait that showed a significantly smaller effect size than the strongest predictor, body masculinity (p < 0.001, q = 0.006).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: 2D:4D showed a significantly smaller effect size on mating than body masculinity (p < 0.001, q = 0.006).
source: The effect for 2D:4D was also nonsignificant (r = 0.034, 95% CI: [0.000, 0.069], q = 0.102), and moderation analyses showed that this was the only trait that showed a significantly smaller effect size than the strongest predictor, body masculinity (p < 0.001, q = 0.006).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic moderation analysis.

claim: Body masculinity was the only trait that significantly predicted the reproductive domain (r = 0.143, 95% CI: [0.076, 0.212], q = 0.001).
source: As Table 3 shows, relationships were generally in the predicted direction, but body masculinity was the strongest and only significant predictor (r = 0.143, 95% CI: [0.076, 0.212], q = 0.001; Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis, with reference to Table 3 and Figure 6.

claim: Height showed a significantly smaller effect size on reproduction than body masculinity (B = –0.107, p = 0.005, q = 0.023).
source: The only trait with an effect size significantly smaller than body masculinity was height (B = –0.107, p = 0.005, q = 0.023).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic moderation analysis.

claim: Most effect sizes (94%) for mating outcomes came from low fertility samples.
source: Across all masculine traits, most effect sizes (94%) came from low fertility samples.
evidence: This is a description of the data distribution in the meta-analysis.

claim: The majority (77%) of observations of reproduction were from high fertility samples.
source: The majority (77 %) of observations of reproduction were from high fertility samples.
evidence: This is a description of the data distribution in the meta-analysis.

claim: Body masculinity effects were stronger in studies where age had not been controlled for compared to where it had been controlled for (B = 0.103, p = 0.015, q = 0.047).
source: Body masculinity effects were stronger in studies where age had not been controlled for compared to where it had been controlled for (B = 0.103, p = 0.015, q = 0.047).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic moderation analysis.

claim: Associations for 2D:4D were weaker in non-white/mixed ethnicity samples compared to white samples (B = –0.080, p = 0.014, q = 0.047).
source: Associations for 2D:4D were weaker in non-white/mixed ethnicity samples compared to white samples (B = –0.080, p = 0.014, q = 0.047), and stronger where variables had been transformed to approximate normality compared to when they had not been transformed (B = 0.103, p = 0.016, q = 0.047).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic moderation analysis.

claim: For body masculinity, body shape was a significantly weaker predictor than strength (B = –0.099, p = 0.003, q = 0.017).
source: For trait-specific moderators, significant moderation was seen for type of body masculinity where body shape was a significantly weaker predictor than strength (B = –0.099, p = 0.003, q = 0.017).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic moderation analysis.

claim: Effects for rated body masculinity were significantly stronger than for indices taken from body measurements (B = 0.177, p = 0.007, q = 0.029).
source: Effects for rated body masculinity were significantly stronger than for indices taken from body measurements (B = 0.177, p = 0.007, q = 0.029).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic moderation analysis.

claim: For body masculinity, the effect on fertility was significant (r = 0.130, 95% CI: [0.060, 0.201], q = 0.002).
source: However, for body masculinity, the effect on fertility was significant (r = 0.130, 95% CI: [0.060, 0.201], q = 0.002; five out of six samples high fertility) while the somewhat larger effect on reproductive success was not.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic subgroup analysis.

claim: For 2D:4D, there was a significant effect for reproductive success (r = 0.174, 95% CI: [0.085, 0.267], q = 0.002).
source: For 2D:4D, there was a significant effect for reproductive success (four out of five samples from high fertility populations: r = 0.174, 95% CI: [0.085, 0.267], q = 0.002) but not for fertility.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic subgroup analysis.

claim: The findings support arguments that strength/muscularity may be sexually selected in humans.
source: Our findings support arguments that strength/muscularity may be sexually selected in humans, but cast doubt regarding selection for other forms of masculinity and highlight the need to increase tests of evolutionary hypotheses outside of industrialized populations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results.

claim: The findings cast doubt regarding selection for other forms of masculinity besides strength/muscularity.
source: Our findings support arguments that strength/muscularity may be sexually selected in humans, but cast doubt regarding selection for other forms of masculinity and highlight the need to increase tests of evolutionary hypotheses outside of industrialized populations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results.

claim: The findings highlight the need to increase tests of evolutionary hypotheses outside of industrialized populations.
source: Our findings support arguments that strength/muscularity may be sexually selected in humans, but cast doubt regarding selection for other forms of masculinity and highlight the need to increase tests of evolutionary hypotheses outside of industrialized populations.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the meta-analytic findings and the distribution of samples.

claim: The findings are consistent with the male-male competition hypothesis.
source: Overall, since traits such as body size, strength, and muscularity are associated with formidability, our findings are consistent with the male-male competition hypothesis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results.

claim: In the Yanomamö Indians, men who kill others have greater reproductive success.
source: For example, in the Yanomamö Indians, men who kill others have greater reproductive success (Chagnon, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Men's facial masculinity exerts virtually no influence on mating when moderated by female choice.
source: Furthermore, the effect of facial masculinity on mating (such as it was) was largely driven by mating attitudes and was close to zero for mating behaviors, suggesting that men's facial masculinity exerts virtually no influence on mating when moderated by female choice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results comparing mating attitudes and behaviors.

claim: The influence of facial masculinity on fertility in high fertility samples was non-existent (r = 0.00).
source: Similarly, the influence of facial masculinity on fertility in high fertility samples was non-existent (r = 0.00).
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: The findings contradict a large body of literature claiming that women's preferences for masculinity in men's faces are adaptive.
source: Overall, these findings contradict a large body of literature claiming that women's preferences for masculinity in men's faces are adaptive.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results.

claim: Women's preferences for facial masculinity (to the extent they exist at all) are a modern anomaly only found in industrialized populations.
source: Rather, they indicate that such preferences (to the extent they exist at all) are a modern anomaly only found in industrialized populations, as suggested by Scott and colleagues (Scott et al., 2014), and as demonstrated by the positive correlation between facial masculinity preferences and national health and human development indices (Marcinkowska et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a positive correlation between facial masculinity preferences and national health and human development indices.
source: Rather, they indicate that such preferences (to the extent they exist at all) are a modern anomaly only found in industrialized populations, as suggested by Scott and colleagues (Scott et al., 2014), and as demonstrated by the positive correlation between facial masculinity preferences and national health and human development indices (Marcinkowska et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The dataset shows a bimodal distribution between studies sampling predominantly English-speaking students and studies sampling foragers, horticulturalists, and other subsistence farmers.
source: One key observation regarding our dataset is that it shows a rather 'bimodal' distribution between a large number of studies sampling (predominantly English-speaking) students on one hand, and a cluster of studies sampling foragers, horticulturalists, and other subsistence farmers (predominantly from just two continents) on the other.
evidence: This is a description of the data distribution in the meta-analysis.

claim: Voice pitch, height, and testosterone levels were associated with self-reported mating success in mostly low fertility populations, but not with actual reproductive fitness in high fertility populations.
source: As noted above, we found that voice pitch, height, and testosterone levels were associated with (largely self-reported) mating success in mostly low fertility populations, but not with actual reproductive fitness in high fertility populations.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: The contradicting pattern of results raises concerns about whether mating measures can be used as reliable indicators of likely ancestral fitness.
source: Overall, however, the contradicting pattern of results for the traits mentioned above raise important concerns for the human sexual selection field, particularly with respect to whether (and which) mating measures can be used as reliable indicators of likely ancestral fitness when considering the current evidence base.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results.

claim: Testosterone levels predicted mating outcomes with similar effect sizes for attitudinal and behavioral measures.
source: As mentioned above, in our analysis testosterone levels predicted mating outcomes – with similar effect sizes for attitudinal and behavioral measures – but did not predict reproduction.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Testosterone levels did not predict reproduction.
source: As mentioned above, in our analysis testosterone levels predicted mating outcomes – with similar effect sizes for attitudinal and behavioral measures – but did not predict reproduction.
evidence: This is a finding from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Testosterone decreases when men enter a relationship or get married.
source: Testosterone also decreases, for example, when men enter a relationship or get married (Archer, 2006; Holmboe et al., 2017), when they become fathers (Archer, 2006; Gettler et al., 2011), or when they engage in childcare (Archer, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Testosterone decreases when men become fathers.
source: Testosterone also decreases, for example, when men enter a relationship or get married (Archer, 2006; Holmboe et al., 2017), when they become fathers (Archer, 2006; Gettler et al., 2011), or when they engage in childcare (Archer, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Testosterone decreases when men engage in childcare.
source: Testosterone also decreases, for example, when men enter a relationship or get married (Archer, 2006; Holmboe et al., 2017), when they become fathers (Archer, 2006; Gettler et al., 2011), or when they engage in childcare (Archer, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: All masculine traits except facial masculinity and 2D:4D were associated with significantly greater mating success.
source: In summary, we used a large-scale meta-analysis of six masculine traits and their relationships with mating and reproductive outcomes to test whether such traits are currently under selection in humans. We found that all masculine traits except facial masculinity and 2D:4D were associated with significantly greater mating success.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: Only body masculinity predicted higher fertility, indexed by reproductive onset, number of offspring, and grand-offspring.
source: However, only body masculinity predicted higher fertility, indexed by reproductive onset, number of offspring, and grand-offspring.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the meta-analytic data analysis.

claim: The mating and reproduction literature is starkly split between studying mating in predominantly student settings and fertility in high fertility settings.
source: We further note that the mating and reproduction literature is starkly split between studying mating in predominantly student settings, and 'only' fertility in high fertility settings, which imposes constraints on both this paper and our field as a whole.
evidence: This is an observation about the distribution of studies in the meta-analysis.

claim: Testing hypotheses about human evolution largely in industrialized populations risks drawing conclusions that are not supported outside of evolutionarily novel contexts.
source: We argue that our findings illustrate that when we test hypotheses about human evolution largely in industrialized populations, we risk drawing conclusions that are not supported outside of evolutionarily novel, highly niche mating and reproductive contexts.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the meta-analytic results and the distribution of samples.
